# R6 Digest — 2 Thessalonians Opening + Thanksgiving (1:1–12)
**Source:** Jeffrey A. D. Weima, *1–2 Thessalonians* (BECNT)
**Reader:** extraction subagent (R6)
**Coverage:** exclusive range source lines 5005–5415 / slice file `R6_2th_opening_thanksgiving_5005-5415.txt` read in full (411 lines; Letter Opening 1:1–2 + Thanksgiving 1:3–12, through Additional Notes on 1:4–1:12; TOC stubs at end only). No material beyond this unit.

## Claims

### C-R6-01 | Letter opening nearly identical to 1 Thessalonians; two noteworthy additions
- **Claim (Weima):** The letter opening of 2 Thessalonians is virtually identical to that of 1 Thessalonians except for two additions that make explicit what was implicit in the previous letter. Like 1 Thessalonians, it is formally simple and unembellished vs. expanded openings (Romans, 1 Cor, Galatians)—likely reflecting the good relationship with the Thessalonian church and absence of questions about Paul’s apostolic status/authority.
- **Quote:** “The letter opening of 2 Thessalonians is virtually identical with that of 1 Thessalonians except for two additions… Compared to the expanded letter opening of Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, or other Pauline Letters, the epistolary conventions… are simple and unembellished. This is likely due to the good relationship that Paul enjoys with the Thessalonian congregation and the absence of any questions in this church about his apostolic status or authority.”
- **Locus:** Opening unit; Literary Analysis; slice ~L1–8 / 2 Thess 1:1–2
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R6-02 | Three functions of the letter opening for the rest of the letter
- **Claim (Weima):** Even this simple opening lays down three points: (1) Silvanus and Timothy as cosenders give further weight/authority—showing Paul is well informed and that there is agreement about the required response; (2) recipients as *ekklēsia* (LXX language for Israel as covenant people) reflects Paul’s view of the predominantly Gentile Thessalonian church as the new people of God; (3) “in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” and the expanded greeting “from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” emphasize the primary role of the divine (God and Christ) in origin, ongoing life, and salvation—comforting for a persecuted and frightened community.
- **Quote:** “the inclusion of Silvanus and Timothy as cosenders gives further weight or authority… the identification of the recipients with the term ekklēsia… reflects Paul’s understanding of the predominantly Gentile church of Thessalonica as the new people of God… Such an emphasis would be comforting for the persecuted and frightened community of believers in Thessalonica.”
- **Locus:** Opening overview; slice ~L3–5 / 2 Thess 1:1–2
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[silas]], [[timothy]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-03 | Cosenders still with Paul; second letter written shortly after the first
- **Claim (Weima):** Mention of Silvanus and Timothy as cosenders indicates they are still with Paul when he writes 2 Thessalonians (cf. 1 Thess 1:1a) and, with the great similarities of openings, strongly suggests the second letter was written relatively briefly after the first.
- **Quote:** “The mention of Silvanus and Timothy as cosenders indicates not only that they are still with Paul when he writes this letter (cf. 1 Thess. 1:1a) but also… strongly suggests that the second letter was written relatively briefly after the first.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a; slice ~L22 / 2 Thess 1:1a
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[silas]], [[timothy]], [[paul-apostle]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]]

### C-R6-04 | Cosenders never re-mentioned is not evidence of pseudonymity
- **Claim (Weima):** Against Trilling and others who treat inclusion of cosenders never again named in the rest of the document as evidence of pseudonymity, Weima calls this “problem” imaginary: in undisputed Paulines, cosenders never re-mentioned include Silvanus (1 Thess 1:1a), Sosthenes (1 Cor 1:1), and Timothy (Philem 1a).
- **Quote:** “Some (Trilling 1972: 35) have viewed the inclusion of these two cosenders as problematic and as further evidence of the letter’s pseudonymity… This “problem,” however, is only imaginary… Silvanus (1 Thess. 1:1a), Sosthenes (1 Cor. 1:1), and Timothy (Philem. 1a).”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a; slice ~L22 / 2 Thess 1:1a
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[silas]], [[timothy]]

### C-R6-05 | Paul is the real author despite cosenders and “we”; plurals literary not literal
- **Claim (Weima):** Cosenders + widespread “we” raise whether Silvanus and Timothy had an active compositional role. Parallel to 1 Thessalonians’ I-shifts (2:18; 3:5; 5:27), 2 Thessalonians has two first-person singular shifts: 2:5 (rhetorical question about what “I” was saying) and especially the autograph greeting 3:17. These strongly imply Paul is the real author; plurals throughout both letters should be taken literarily, not literally.
- **Quote:** “These texts strongly imply that, though the names of Silvanus and Timothy are included as cosenders, Paul is the real author and that the plurals used throughout both letters ought to be taken literarily, not literally.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a; slice ~L24 / 2 Thess 1:1a (with 2:5; 3:17)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[paul-apostle]], [[silas]], [[timothy]], [[2-thessalonians]]

### C-R6-06 | Addition of “our” Father in recipient formula: adoption, warmth, anti-cool-tone argument
- **Claim (Weima):** First addition vs. 1 Thess opening: possessive “our” with God in the recipient formula—God as Father of believers (senders and recipients), not Father of Christ or of creation. Creates solidarity and warmth/intimacy; overlooked by those who claim 2 Thessalonians has a cooler tone than 1 Thessalonians and use that for non-Pauline authorship. Also comforts persecuted readers as family of God, not facing trials alone as pagans.
- **Quote:** “this fact is overlooked by many who claim that 2 Thessalonians has a decidedly cooler tone than 1 Thessalonians and go on to use this claimed difference as further grounds for accepting non-Pauline authorship of the second letter… the Thessalonians are hereby reminded… that they face their trials not alone as pagans but as a community… brought into the family of God, their spiritual Father.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:1b; slice ~L29–33 / 2 Thess 1:1b
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-07 | Second addition: explicit source of grace and peace; double God/Christ reference not pseudepigraphic
- **Claim (Weima):** Second difference: greeting expanded with “from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” so both opening verses end with nearly identical God-and-Christ phrases. Against Richard’s view of an “anomalous, ponderous double reference” as pseudepigraphic strategy, Weima notes parallel back-to-back God/Christ references in undisputed Paul (e.g. 2 Cor 1:2–3; Gal 1:1, 3). Repetition rhetorically emphasizes divine role in origin and ongoing life—comfort for the persecuted.
- **Quote:** “Instead of viewing the double reference to God and Christ as problematic, it should instead be recognized that this repetition functions rhetorically to emphasize the primary and thus crucial role of the Divine… Such an emphasis is comforting for the persecuted and frightened community of believers in Thessalonica.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:2; slice ~L37–40 / 2 Thess 1:2
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-08 | Single-preposition juxtaposition of God and Christ implies high Christology
- **Claim (Weima):** Both divine persons function as double object of a single preposition; juxtaposition without explanation/justification implies high Christology assumed in missionary preaching and accepted by readers. Cites Wilson via Morris; Fee on monotheist pressure of such Christ-speech in both Thessalonian letters.
- **Quote:** “That such a construction could be used without comment not only implies the writer’s belief in the deity of Christ, but also takes the reader’s acknowledgment of it for granted” (Wilson, cited by Morris). Fee: “this rigorous monotheist can speak about Christ in ways as remarkable as one finds here—statements that by their very nature would seem to put considerable pressure on that monotheism.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:2; slice ~L42 / 2 Thess 1:2
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-09 | Textual note on “our” in 1:2: omission weakens pseudepigraphy claims
- **Claim (Weima):** Prefers omission of possessive “our” in 1:2 on external + internal (shorter) evidence; scribes later added to match other Pauline greetings. If omitted, weakens pseudepigraphy: Fee asks whether a pseudepigrapher would “botch the borrowing” of this phrase from the rest of the corpus.
- **Quote:** “If, as seems likely, the pronoun should be omitted, this weakens the claims of this letter’s supposed pseudepigraphical character, since, as Fee (2007: 69n113) asks: “Would a pseudepigrapher have thus botched the borrowing of this phrase from the rest of the corpus?””
- **Locus:** Additional Note 1:2; slice ~L46 / 2 Thess 1:2
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-10 | Thanksgiving 1:3–12: three functions (pastoral, paraenetic, foreshadowing)
- **Claim (Weima):** Pauline thanksgivings serve pastoral, paraenetic/exhortative, and foreshadowing functions—all at work in 2 Thess 1:3–12. Pastoral: reestablishes relationship via gratitude for growth of faith and love despite opposition. Paraenetic: challenges (implicitly 3–10; explicitly prayer report 11–12) to live up to praise and petitions. Foreshadowing: anticipates the letter body’s main eschatological issue—false claim that the day of the Lord has come (2:1–17)—while the body’s overriding concern is comfort of shaken believers, already foreshadowed here.
- **Quote:** “First, it has a pastoral function… Second, it has a paraenetic, or exhortative, function… Third, it has a foreshadowing function: the thanksgiving anticipates the eschatological issue… the false claim that the day of the Lord has already come (2:1–17)… the apostle’s overriding concern is not so much to correct this false teaching as it is to comfort the shaken believers.”
- **Locus:** Thanksgiving intro; slice ~L64 / 2 Thess 1:3–12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-11 | Tripartite structure of thanksgiving: 3–4 / 5–10 / 11–12
- **Claim (Weima):** Thanksgiving falls into three units: (A) 3–4 commendation for spiritual growth under persecution; (B) 5–10 comfort via “just judgment of God” (punishment of persecutors; reward of persecuted); (C) 11–12 prayer-report challenge stressing divine initiative. Overriding concern of 2 Thessalonians is “not to calculate the future but to comfort the church,” already at work in the thanksgiving. Concentric-structure claims for the three units are not strongly enough supported.
- **Quote:** “To put it in colloquial terms, Paul’s overriding concern in 2 Thessalonians is not to calculate the future but to comfort the church, and this consolatory purpose is at work already in the thanksgiving section.”
- **Locus:** Structure / Exegesis intro; slice ~L66–71, 110–132, 142 / 2 Thess 1:3–12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R6-12 | Extent of thanksgiving unit clearly marked (1:3–12)
- **Claim (Weima):** Opening at v. 3: greeting ends letter opening; key verb “to give thanks” at head of sentence (even as “We ought to give thanks”); vocative “brothers” as transitional device. Closing after v. 12: prayer report closes other Pauline thanksgivings; glorification language echoes eschatological v. 10; 2:1 opens with appeal formula + vocative “brothers.”
- **Quote:** “The extent of this thanksgiving section is not in dispute; both its opening and conclusion are clearly marked.”
- **Locus:** Literary Analysis “Extent of the Passage”; slice ~L80–84 / 2 Thess 1:3–12; 2:1
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-13 | Style of 5–10: asyndeton, dik- root coherence, OT allusions not a preformed hymn/testimony collection
- **Claim (Weima):** Vv. 5–10 differ formally and stylistically (asyndeton; heavy eschatology; divine action vs. human action in 3–4); lexical coherence via dik- root four times and “give (back)” with justice. Hymn-of-Second-Coming and Isa-66-conscious-reflection / testimony-collection theories have not found wide acceptance; most take OT parallels as unconscious allusions from Paul himself. Section also frequently employs contrastive and synonymous parallelism.
- **Quote:** “most commentators view the OT parallels in 1:5–10 to be the result of unconscious allusions that come from the hand of the apostle himself rather than any preformed tradition.”
- **Locus:** Structure of the Passage; slice ~L90–94 / 2 Thess 1:5–10
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-14 | Thanksgiving obligation: “we ought” / “as it is fitting” not cool distance or non-Pauline
- **Claim (Weima):** Rejects multiple explanations of “we ought… as it is fitting”: (1) response to Thessalonian letter of unworthiness (Frame/Bruce/Morris—too speculative mirror-reading); (2) anti-flattery response to 1 Thess 2 opponents (D. Martin—speculative); (3) liturgical formula alone (Aus—why only here?); (4) cool/distant language as non-Pauline evidence (Dibelius, Bailey, Trilling, Furnish)—founders on subsequent warm intimacy (“brothers”) and exuberant commendation (faith “growing abundantly,” boasting to other churches). Best: common Jewish/Christian theme of obligation to thank God (m. Pesaḥ. 10.5; 1 Clem. 38.4; Barn. 7.1); shift from simple “We give thanks” because growth amid opposition is remarkable and comforts sufferers.
- **Quote:** “this interpretation founders on the fact that the subsequent language of the thanksgiving is not only very warm and intimate (note the presence of the vocative “brothers”) but even exuberant in its commendation… the apostle is simply acknowledging… the need for gratitude to be given to God since he is responsible for the growth of faith and love.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:3; slice ~L146–161 / 2 Thess 1:3
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-15 | Theocentric thanksgiving: growth due to God, not human credit
- **Claim (Weima):** Though the Thessalonians are subject matter of thanksgiving, the theology is theocentric—thanks “to God,” parallel to 1 Thess thanksgiving where faith/love/hope, exemplary life, evangelism, conversion, and missionary genuineness are ultimately due to election. Rest of 2 Thess thanksgiving likewise: God’s vindication/punishment (5–10); prayer to “our God” (11–12); second thanksgiving 2:13–14 on election/call.
- **Quote:** “even though the church is commended for the abundant increase of their faith and love… all this remarkable spiritual growth is ultimately due to God’s activity in their lives, and so God is the one to whom thanksgiving must be given.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:3; slice ~L163 / 2 Thess 1:3
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-16 | Vocative “brothers” and “always”: kinship warmth continues from 1 Thessalonians
- **Claim (Weima):** “Always concerning you” is formulaic yet gains credibility from vocative “brothers,” not typically part of thanksgiving (only Thessalonian correspondence). Heavy kinship language in 1 Thess carries into this letter written shortly later; with emphatic “we ourselves” (v. 4) stresses affectionate bond (Malherbe).
- **Quote:** “The use of the vocative “brothers” here in a letter written to the same audience only a short time later… continues this use of kinship language and… stresses the affectionate nature of the relationship that exists between Paul and his readers.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:3; slice ~L165 / 2 Thess 1:3
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]]

### C-R6-17 | Faith growing abundantly: hyperauxanei and letter-long faith emphasis
- **Claim (Weima):** First causal reason for thanksgiving: faith “growing abundantly” (*hyperauxanei*, only here in NT)—compound *hyper* marks unusual/unexpected progress (O’Brien); present tense ongoing growth. Faith was major concern in 1 Thess (1:3; 3:2, 5–7, 10; 5:8); emphasis continues in 2 Thess thanksgiving (faith again in v. 4 with persecution; v. 11 prayer; verbal “believe” twice in v. 10). Giblin sees main theme of 1:3–12 as “fulfillment of faith” and titles 2:1–17 “The Threat to Faith.”
- **Quote:** “this form of the verb “points to the unusual, even unexpected, progress of the addressees’ faith.” … Giblin… considers the main theme of 1:3–12 to be “the fulfillment of faith”… and who titles his exposition of 2:1–17 as “The Threat to Faith.””
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:3; slice ~L169–173 / 2 Thess 1:3
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-18 | Love of each one of you all for one another increasing
- **Claim (Weima):** Second reason: love of each one of all for one another is increasing—phrase without parallel in Paul/NT; Morris: “Clearly Paul is making no exceptions.” Love was major 1 Thess concern (1:2–3; 2:17–3:10; 3:6, 12; 4:9–12; 5:8, 12–22). Commendation is surprising given rebellious idlers (3:6–15) exploiting love/generosity—Bruce: uncharacteristic minority; Paul still ends idler treatment with “not be discouraged in doing good” (3:13) and admonish as brother not enemy (3:15). Praise also has paraenetic pressure to continue growing in faith and love.
- **Quote:** “The expression is a strong one. Clearly Paul is making no exceptions. Love was a bond uniting the whole church.” … “these idlers must constitute “an uncharacteristic minority”…”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:3; slice ~L175–181 / 2 Thess 1:3 (with 3:6–15)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-19 | Boasting to the churches of God about steadfastness and faith under persecution
- **Claim (Weima):** Result clause: emphatic “we ourselves” + rare compound *enkauchasthai* (only NT occurrence) + present tense = continuous public boasting “in the churches of God” about “steadfastness and faith” in “all your persecutions and afflictions” they are enduring. Intensive “we ourselves” need not contrast another boasting party (rejects Bruce/others, Morris/others, Malherbe/Frame humility proposals). “Churches of God” without geography = general reference to churches with which Paul had contact (possibly Judea, Achaia, “every place”). One article for “steadfastness and faith” links the qualities closely (not hendiadys of “patient endurance” alone).
- **Quote:** “to the persecuted community of believers in Thessalonica, it will be comforting to hear that their founder, Paul, is so proud of their remarkable spiritual growth that he not only gives thanks to God for them but also boasts about them to other believers, both far and near.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:4; slice ~L183–199 / 2 Thess 1:4
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[1-thessalonians]]

### C-R6-20 | Ongoing persecution: social harassment not martyrdom; intensified since 1 Thessalonians
- **Claim (Weima):** *Diōgmos* + *thlipsis* together for rhetorical effect of religious persecution; “all” + present *anechesthe* = numerous ongoing incidents, not past only. Persecution from conversion onward (1 Thess 1:6; Acts 17:5–9) continued after missionaries left; still present and seems more intense at writing of 2 Thessalonians. Opposition likely severe social harassment and ostracism, not physical death/martyrdom (Still 1999).
- **Quote:** “this opposition to the fledgling Christian movement in Thessalonica has still not stopped but is a present reality that actually seems to have become more intense… this opposition likely did not involve physical death and martyrdom but brought severe social harassment and ostracism (Still 1999).”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:4; slice ~L200–207 / 2 Thess 1:4
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-21 | “Evidence of the just judgment of God” (1:5): prospective reading preferred
- **Claim (Weima):** Rejects traditional retrospective reading (endurance = evidence; Lightfoot, Frame, Best, Bruce, Morris, Fee, etc.) and Bassler et al. “theology of suffering” reading (persecutions themselves as just temporary punishment of elect)—latter lacks strong match in Jewish sources as used, Paul says nothing about few sins of the good, idea not elsewhere in Paul, Gentile readers unlikely to catch it. Prefers prospective reading: v. 5 is apodosis of conditional beginning at eiper (v. 6); “evidence” is the equitable future punishment of afflicters and reward of afflicted spelled out in 6–10 (brief then fuller). Judgment is end-time, not present-only (corrective to false claim day of Lord has come, 2:2).
- **Quote:** ““Here is the evidence of the just judgment of God,” with the actual evidence found not in the preceding verse (1:4) but in the following verses (1:6–10).” … “the “just judgment of God” must refer to an end-time event… The future aspect of the judgment is an important corrective to the false claim… that the day of the Lord has already come (2:2).”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:5; slice ~L214–233 / 2 Thess 1:5
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]]

### C-R6-22 | Made worthy of the kingdom; suffering “on behalf of” the kingdom with the writers
- **Claim (Weima):** Consequence of just future judgment: divine passive *kataxiōthēnai*—God will make them worthy of the kingdom (here predominantly future at Christ’s return; cf. 1 Thess 2:12). Relative clause: present suffering acknowledged pastorally; *kai* points to shared suffering with writers (*meth’ hēmōn* in v. 7); *hyper* = suffering “for/on behalf of” the kingdom, not means of achieving membership.
- **Quote:** “although the Thessalonian believers are suffering now, God’s future judgment is just, and this means that he… will ensure that they are made worthy of full participation in the blessedness of his eschatological rule.” … “the idea is one of suffering “for” or “on behalf of” the kingdom.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:5; slice ~L235–245 / 2 Thess 1:5
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-23 | Eschatological reversal briefly: affliction to afflicters; rest to the afflicted with us (1:6–7a)
- **Claim (Weima):** *Eiper* = “since” (assumed fact): just in God’s sight to pay back (*antapodounai*, emphatic double preposition; lex talionis / Isa 66:6, 15 echo possible) affliction to those afflicting them. Pastoral purpose drives language, not theodicy theory (Malherbe). Positive parallel: rest (*anesis*) to the afflicted “with us”—eschatological relief, not mere inactivity; includes reunion with Paul, Silvanus, Timothy who share affliction. Contrasting parallel sharpens fitting justice of each group’s outcome.
- **Quote:** “It is this practical, pastoral purpose that drives Paul’s language, not an interest in divine retribution as part of theodicy.” … “they too—in keeping with the just judgment of God—will share with the readers in the eschatological blessing of “rest.””
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:6–7a; slice ~L249–286 / 2 Thess 1:6–7a
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[silas]], [[timothy]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]

### C-R6-24 | Harsh judgment language and God’s justice not opposed to mercy
- **Claim (Weima):** “Affliction” to afflicters is among Paul’s harshest judgment language; some stumble over it vs. merciful God. Weima cites Heidelberg Catechism Q/A 11 and Marshall: NT does not suggest God’s love is indifferent to justice or freely pardons persecutors at the cost of failing to defend the persecuted.
- **Quote:** “Nothing in the NT suggests that God’s love is indifferent to justice, and that he bestows a free pardon on his enemies at the cost of failing to defend the persecuted against the persecutors.” (Marshall, endorsed in context)
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:6; slice ~L260–261 / 2 Thess 1:6
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]

### C-R6-25 | Timing and manner: revelation of Lord Jesus from heaven with angels in flame of fire (1:7b–8a)
- **Claim (Weima):** Judgment timing: *en tē apokalypsei tou kyriou Iēsou*—temporal “at the revelation,” not merely instrumental. *Apokalypsis* (vs. preferred *parousia* elsewhere) stresses revelatory aspect: Judge currently hidden from persecutors; known to believers who endure until manifestation. Three modifiers establish authority/power: from heaven (divine authority); “angels of his power” (preferred reading: power mediated through angels; Marshall: precise force less important than impression of divine power); “in a flame of fire” (Weima prefers *en phlogi pyros*, Isa 66:15 judgment imagery over Exod 3:2 theophany assimilation).
- **Quote:** “the truth that Jesus the Judge will come to carry out the just judgment of God is a reality currently hidden from those persecuting the Thessalonian believers… Conversely, since this truth is known to the Christians in Thessalonica, they are able to endure persecution until the “revelation of the Lord Jesus.””
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:7b–8a; slice ~L288–304 / 2 Thess 1:7b–8a
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[1-thessalonians]]

### C-R6-26 | Christ as agent of divine punishment; single group of the punished (1:8)
- **Claim (Weima):** “Inflicting punishment” (*didontes ekdikēsin*)—third dik- root use—transfers to returning Christ an action LXX ascribes to God (esp. Isa 66:15). Targets not only local persecutors but generically “those who do not know God and… do not obey the gospel.” Rejects two-group (Gentiles/Jews) reading; synonymous parallelism yields one group of all who fail to know God and obey the gospel.
- **Quote:** “the divine work of meting out the just judgment of God is transferred to the returning Christ… Therefore it is best to see Paul as describing a single group consisting of all those who will justly be punished for their failure to know God and obey the gospel.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:8; slice ~L306–312 / 2 Thess 1:8
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]

### C-R6-27 | Eternal destruction from the presence of the Lord (1:9)—unending ruin not annihilation
- **Claim (Weima):** Fourth dik- root: “pay a penalty” (*dikēn tisousin*)—just legal penalty stressed by word order. Elaborated as “eternal destruction from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might” (Isa 2:10, 19, 21 echo; “fear” omitted for better parallelism; presence/glory language applied to Lord Jesus). *Olethron aiōnion* = unending ruin/continuing punishment, not annihilation—argued from Jesus tradition, Jewish heritage, and parallel phrases presupposing ongoing existence. Description more general/vague than Jewish apocalyptic detail because pastoral “evidence of just judgment,” not precise retribution theology. Separation from Lord’s presence is for Paul the worst prospect; other fiery images elsewhere are symbols.
- **Quote:** “That Paul does not have in view a destruction of a person that lasts forever (i.e., their annihilation) but rather their unending ruin (i.e., their continuing punishment) seems clear from three factors…” … “To be separated from God and his blessings—and to be forever in this situation—is for Paul the worst of prospects.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:9; slice ~L314–325 / 2 Thess 1:9
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-28 | Lex talionis pastoral logic: punishment fits crime; reward fits deed
- **Claim (Weima):** Purpose is not hyperbolic depiction so readers maliciously rejoice over oppressors’ fate, but to show judgment is just: those who separate from God in this life are justly separated hereafter; those who endure affliction receive rest (v. 7) and glorification (v. 10)—“the punishment fits the crime” / “the reward fits the deed.”
- **Quote:** “his larger purpose in this section of the letter is to give evidence that God’s judgment is just, or in colloquial terms, that “the punishment fits the crime”… Conversely and comfortingly, “the reward fits the deed.””
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:9; slice ~L323 / 2 Thess 1:9
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-29 | Positive judgment: Christ glorified and marveled at in his holy ones / all who believe (1:10)
- **Claim (Weima):** “Whenever he comes” (indefinite timing, not doubt of reality) + two synonymous infinitives: glorified in his holy ones (Ps 89:7 / 88:8 LXX applied to Christ; “holy ones” = believers, not angels, per parallel “all who believe”); marveled at in all who believe (Ps 68:35 / 67:36 LXX). Locative *en* preferred (presence of believers), matching Ps, parallel clause, and contrast with exclusion “from the presence of the Lord” (v. 9). “All” + parenthetical “because our testimony to you was believed” reassures Thessalonians they belong among the blessed—addressing ongoing anxiety about salvation status (cf. 1 Thess 5:1–11; false day-of-Lord claim in 2:1–17). Closing “on that day” (day of the Lord) foreshadows 2:1–17: no need to be disturbed that the day “has come,” since it cannot occur until this just judgment is carried out.
- **Quote:** “This was a word of comfort for the congregation as a whole, but especially for those who wondered about the state of their salvation.” … “There is no need for the Thessalonian Christians to be disturbed by a claim that “the day of the Lord has come” (2:2), since that eschatological event cannot take place until the judgment of God has been carried out.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:10; slice ~L327–341 / 2 Thess 1:10
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-30 | Prayer report 1:11–12: challenge + consolation; foreshadows body concerns
- **Claim (Weima):** Formal “prayer report” (not optative direct prayer) closing thanksgiving; paraenetic challenge to live up to prayed standard, yet consoling via knowing Paul prays and via divine initiative. Foreshadows letter body: v. 11 present conduct → 3:1–15 (esp. rebellious idleness); v. 12 end-time glorification → 2:1–17. “To this end” (*eis ho*) looks back to whole of 5–10’s just judgment message, not only v. 5 worthiness or v. 10 salvation. *Kai* links praying always to giving thanks always (v. 3), not reciprocal prayer or letter from fainthearted.
- **Quote:** “God is the one who will make them worthy of their election and who will complete their good desire and work, thereby ensuring that both the Lord Jesus Christ and they will be glorified.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:11–12 intro; slice ~L343–350 / 2 Thess 1:11–12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-31 | Two petitions: make worthy of the calling; complete desire of goodness and work of faith in power (1:11)
- **Claim (Weima):** *Hina* supplies content of prayer. (1) “Our God may make you worthy of the calling”—*axioō* as “make worthy” (not merely “consider”) because of divine subject and Pauline theology (Marshall); *klēsis* is past divine call (not future prize), as throughout Thessalonian correspondence (2 Thess 2:14; 1 Thess 1:4; 2:12; 4:7; 5:9, 24)—present conduct demonstrating positive response to past call. (2) God “complete” every desire of goodness (human desire from goodness; subjective genitive; interest in others’ well-being) and work of faith (subjective: work produced by faith; cf. 1 Thess 1:3; Gal 5:6)—progress from will to deed (Frame/O’Brien); “in power” brackets out merit claims while requiring human action (Malherbe).
- **Quote:** “God cannot deem worthy any whom he himself has not made worthy by his action rather than by their good works; hence the force of the verb is tantamount to ‘make worthy.’” … “The second petition is bracketed by reference to God’s activity, which rules out any possible claim to merit, yet it requires human action.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:11; slice ~L355–366 / 2 Thess 1:11
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-32 | Purpose of prayer: name of Lord Jesus glorified in you and you in him (1:12)—eschatological mutual glorification
- **Claim (Weima):** *Hopōs* purposes (plural) shift to future: name of Lord Jesus glorified in you and you in him—allusion to Isa 66:5 (fitting for despised/mockedsufferers). Glorification is eschatological at second coming (parallel rare compound *endoxazō* with v. 10; believer glorification usually future; thanksgivings end futuristically; whole tenor of 1:3ff eschatological—Best), not present via instrumental “through your actions.” Locative *en hymin* // “in his holy ones.” V. 12 uniquely adds glorification of believers themselves (“and you in him”)—vindication plus transformation into glory (body transformation; creation liberation background). “Name” not over-theologized: simply from Isa 66:5 (Marshall).
- **Quote:** “God is changing believers now (v. 11) so that glorification can take place at the End.” … “the Thessalonian Christians will not only have their faith vindicated when they are personally present and participate in the eschatological glorification of Christ but will also themselves be glorified.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:12; slice ~L368–378 / 2 Thess 1:12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R6-33 | Closing grace formula: two figures (God and Lord Jesus Christ), not Sharp-rule identification
- **Claim (Weima):** “According to the grace of our God and of our Lord Jesus Christ”—single article for two nouns does not (contra Turner/Green Sharp-rule readings and some versions) identify Jesus as “our God and Lord”; Sharp excludes personal names and “Lord” functions nearly as personal name; anarthrous “Lord” common in Thessalonians. Two distinct figures: grace from God (echo 1:2; divine initiative of v. 11) mediated through Christ, whose return is the moment of reward/punishment.
- **Quote:** “It is more likely that Paul has two distinct figures in view in describing the work of grace.”
- **Locus:** Exegesis 1:12; slice ~L380 / 2 Thess 1:12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]]

### C-R6-34 | Authorship/tone synthesis across 1:1–12 (Weima’s cumulative stance)
- **Claim (Weima):** Across opening and thanksgiving, Weima consistently rebuts cooler-tone / formal-distance / double-God-Christ / cosender / obligatory-thanks arguments for non-Pauline authorship: cosenders and brief interval after 1 Thess; “our Father” and “brothers” warm; obligation language common and still exuberant; “we” literary with I-shifts and autograph 3:17; text-critical omission of “our” in 1:2 awkward for a careful forger. Consolatory purpose unifies the unit and anticipates 2:1–17.
- **Quote:** (composite loci) cooler-tone claim “overlooked” by warmth of “our” (L33); obligation-as-non-Pauline “founders on… very warm and intimate” language (L157); “plurals… literarily, not literally” (L24); “not to calculate the future but to comfort the church” (L142).
- **Locus:** Opening + Thanksgiving passim; slice ~L1–46, 64–71, 146–165, 142
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[2-thessalonians]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

- **Read in full:** slice lines 1–411 corresponding to source range 5005–5415: Letter Opening (1:1–2) with Literary Analysis, Exegesis (Sender/Recipient/Greeting), Additional Note 1:2; full Thanksgiving (1:3–12) with Literary Analysis (character, extent, structure, outline), Exegesis A 1:3–4, B 1:5–10 (assertion; brief evidence 6–7a; fuller 7b–10), C prayer report 1:11–12; Additional Notes 1:4, 1:8, 1:10, 1:11, 1:12; trailing TOC stubs only (no new exposition).
- **Not in range:** 2 Thess 2:1–17 body exposition beyond foreshadowing comments; full treatment of rebellious idlers beyond cross-references; 1 Thess letter-opening full comments (Weima defers reader there).
- **Claim count:** 34 (within ~25–40 target). All claims Weima-attributed with verbatim anchors; no live wiki writes.
